Investors reacted with fear that a Democratic Congress, and states across the country, would crack down on artificial intelligence and data centers. This is a market reaction. It is not a new law. Now the front page. A judge has blocked construction of Trump's arch for fourteen days. The order came just after a federal panel approved the project late Thursday. In Paraguay, lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after he resigned. A digital bank tied to his government collapsed, and millions of people's savings were frozen. The Lever reports on a 181-page plan urging Democrats to put tech executives, Wall Street landlords and price gougers under oath. Corporate Democrats are pushing back. And in Atlanta, vertical construction has begun on the next Buckhead Village tower, after deep foundation work wrapped. Now the sections. In tech, Claude Console has a new beta IP allowlist. It limits where a leaked API key can be used. In politics, The Lever says the Democratic landslide strengthens Hakeem Jeffries' bid for speaker. In world news, Pope Leo the Fourteenth began a three-nation Latin America tour in Uruguay. That comes three weeks after lung cancer surgery. In sports, the Rockets, now seven and two, play the Suns, who are two and five. The 49ers are getting wide receivers back from injury as the trade deadline nears. In Atlanta, Atlanta Housing is close to its goal of ten thousand affordable homes. It reports nine thousand seven hundred seventy-six created or preserved since July 2022. In architecture, Autom8Labs launched skills that guide AI agents through tasks in Revit, AutoCAD and Grasshopper. In science, lab octopuses showed the moves they use to squeeze through tiny holes. The finding could inspire soft robot designs. That is the brief. Have a good day.

lead.title: Fears of an AI crackdown after midterms spark $2 trillion rout in tech stocks
lead.note: Technology stocks fell sharply after the midterm elections, with a loss in value of about two trillion dollars. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent. According to the report, investors reacted with fear that a Democratic Congress, along with states across the country, would crack down on artificial intelligence and data centers. The story is about a market reaction, not a policy change. It describes what investors expect, not any law that has passed. For a reader who builds tools with AI and follows the industry, it shows how closely markets now link the future of AI companies to election results and regulation. It is worth watching whether the fear turns into specific proposals on AI or data centers in the months ahead. The summary does not say which companies lost the most or which measures might come first.
